From deep space to deep waters, Star Trek IV: The Voyage Home engages the ever-stalwart crew of the U.S.S. Enterprise in a humanistic quest that begins and ends in the twenty-third century but unfolds for the most part in modern-day San Francisco. Along with its customary quota of spaceships and transporter beams, the latest adventure called for a representation of the planet Vulcan, a unique time travel effect, major storm sequences on earth and a totally convincing simulation of two humpback whales. Now, another decade later, the long-suffering ape has been resurrected once more for King Kong Lives - again as an ape-suited actor augmented by full-size mechanical artifacts. Discussing their work on the film are creature creator Carlo Rambaldi, production designer Peter Murton, visual effects supervisor Barry Nolan, and model shop supervisors David Jones and Dave Kelsey. No science fiction or fantasy world ever created has been more warmly or enthusiastically embraced by its fans than the singular world of Star Trek. Despite premature cancellation as a network television series, Star Trek's phenomenal popularity has kept it on the air for more than twenty years, spawning in the process a full-scale motion picture and three sequels. Achieving an unprecedented continuity, the same actors have played the same characters aboard the same starship for all of those twenty-some years. Though not all of the films have been especially well-received by critics, each has generated long lines at the boxoffice thanks to a vast audience still eager to reunite with old friends. In Star Trek IV: The Voyage Home, the series seems at last to have hit its stride, blending elements of tonguein-cheek humor, adventure, romance, fantasy - in short, everything that made the television series beloved in the first place. Clearly, the crew of the U.S.S. Enterprise has come home. In the story devised by director Leonard Nimoy and producer Harve Bennett, Admiral James T. Kirk and his faithful crew have opted to return to earth and face the consequences of their defiant rescue of Spock in Star Trek III. En route, however, they pick up a distress signal warning them of an alien probe that has neutralized earth's defenses and initiated a stream of transmissions which - left unanswered - will soon destroy the planet's atmosphere and oceans. Discovering a correlation between the alien signals and the song of the now extinct humpback whale, the enterprising star travelers journey back through time to the twentieth century, hoping to return with a pair of humpbacks that can somehow respond to the probe. As scripted, Star Trek IV covers more galactic ground than any of its predecessors - moving from Vulcan to twenty-third century San Francisco to twentieth century San Francisco to the oceanic world of humpback whales. Star Trek was leaving the domain of fantasy to enter the real world as we know it - something that had been done in its low-budget television days but not since its progression to grand-scale filmmaking. The challenge in creating the special effects for the film lay within that realism. In fact, by far the most worrisome effects aspects of the movie - for Nimoy, Bennett and the executives at Paramount - were not the futuristic sequences but rather those taking place in the year 1986. Industrial Light and Magic had already bravely gone where only one other company had gone before by producing effects for both Star Trek II and III, and Paramount was more than happy to engage their services again. Visual consultant Ralph McQuarrie had been hired to conceptualize many of Nimoy's and Bennett's ideas, sharing duties with ILM art director Nilo Rodis. One of Rodis' first designs was for the probe which emerges mysteriously out of a starfield as the film begins. Incorporating ideas he received from the filmmakers in Los Angeles, Rodis devised a vaguely whalelike cylinder that was exceptionally simple - in fact, it was its stark simplicity that the effects crew would ultimately find most troublesome. "I think the probe was the most difficult thing we had to work with on this show," Don Dow stated, "simply because there was nothing to it. Our original instructions from L.A. were to make it 'menacing, military and massive' and it was supposed to appear to be about five miles long and a mile-anda-half wide. To really do that, we would have had to build a model that was as big as a building. And because it was so devoid of detail, I was afraid it was just going to look like a giant water heater in space." The task of producing the probe fell to the ILM model shop. "Since Nilo's concept was that the probe looked similar to a whale," model shop supervisor Jeff Mann explained, "we built a prototype that was a cylinder shape with barnacles and whalelike coloring - but still basically just a tube. We capped the ends of a piece of irrigation pipe and installed a mechanism to turn the ball-like antenna that jutted out from the bottom. Our primary probe model was eight feet long, but we also made a small one for the long-distance shots and another big section that was a forced perspective model - about twenty feet long and really wide at one end and then tapered back at the other. That was for a Star Wars type shot of the probe coming over the heads of the audience, and it really made it look massive - as if it went on forever. We also built an antenna to go with that one that was about a foot-and-a-half in diameter." To conserve on optical time, the effects crew was determined to do as much in-camera work as possible. Jeff Mann adhered to this philosophy, producing all the lighting effects on the probe practically. "The probe had a hole on the bottom that the ball jutted out from. Inside it, we put six halogen bulbs that emitted a general glow down onto the ball and out the hole. Then, down the center we had a tube of plexiglass that was about two inches in diameter that attached to the ball. Inside of that was a long tube lamp - like a refrigerator lamp - which was just screwed into a 110 socket. So the stage crew could do several light passes on the probe. First they would do a pass on the glow of the six halogen bulbs, taking a piece of diffusion material and putting it in the hole. Then we took the diffusion material off and they shot another exposure with the tube light going down the center. A third light pass was of the ball, which was transparent. We built it out of plastic, took a mold off of it and cast it in high-heat epoxy and hooked a rig inside of it. After several failed attempts to get a sufficiently menacing image from the initial whale-colored probe, it was decided that a new paint job and some detail had to be added to its essentially characterless surface. "We had to give it some texture." Dow said. "After brainstorming it for a while, Ken Ralston came up with the idea of painting it shiny black and then backlighting it so there would be reflections coming off of it. We also ended up pock-marking the surface a little so that the backlighting would pick up some hills and valleys. Then we shot it with fog filters which helped to give it an awesome, mysterious quality." Though the probe and its antenna had been lit practically, the optical department still made a major contribution, both enhancing and correcting the shots. "The spherical antenna underneath the probe was originally shot so that it was orange." optical supervisor Ralph Gordon commented, "which unfortunately made it look very much like a spinning basketball. So we pulled mattes off of that one element to drop it out - the ball itself had been shot separately from the probe - and then we made high-con elements that allowed us to expose blue light over that same area. We threw in all sorts of diffusion and filters on it to break up the image and give it a glow that looked like it was coming from the inside. That took a lot of finagling. We put diffusions on both the main projector head of our optical printer and on the aerial head, the back projector. We'd find a diffusion that worked somewhere, lock that off and then move the back head around trying to figure out where the best placement of the diffusion was. Like always, it was just a matter of trial and error." For both the film characters and the effects crews, the probe was an unknown. Fortunately, the spacecraft it encountered were more familiar. In fact, no new ship designs were required for Star Trek IV- and for the most part, old miniatures were simply brought out of moth balls. The U.S.S. Saratoga - the first Starfleet vessel to encounter the probe - was actually the old Reliant from Star Trek III, reworked, renamed and reemployed. Although the motion control model of the Bird of Prey - the Klingon ship abducted by Kirk and his crew - was also a holdover (from Star Trek II and III), the ILM model shop was required to build some simpler but sturdier versions for crashes and other action sequences. "A motion control model is an elaborate, expensive thing," Mann asserted, "and you don't want to be throwing it around. In this latest film, the Bird of Prey had to do a lot of different things - crashing in the water under the Golden Gate Bridge, for example. It was also, originally, going to come around the sun in the time travel sequence and fly right by the camera on fire, with flames streaking out behind it. So we built some practical Bird of Prey models - ones that could withstand the crashing and the water. We did that by taking the motion control model apart and making molds off of all the parts. From those molds, we made a nose and body part out of fiberglass so that it would be really strong. We also built crude aluminum armatures that could articulate the three positions of the wings - up for landing, straight for flying and down for attacking. The wings were made out of furniture foam - a very dense, strong foam that is used for the arms of furniture. These models were very simple - without lights or anything on them - and were meant to be used only for the rough stuff." Though exterior shots of the Bird of Prey were obtained with models, a full-size set had to be constructed for its interior. Working closely with production designer Jack T. Collis and his art department, physical effects supervisor Michael Lantieri tried to create an atmosphere within the ship that was Klingonlike, yet different than previously presented. "Leonard told us to keep the look of the Bird of Prey down," Lantieri said, "so we used an overall ambient haze of smoke inside the ship to give it the look of a trash barrel in space. We also stayed with the angular look of the Klingons, being very careful to pick only triangles and right-angle components - even the digits are at an angle. So we definitely kept to a Klingon theme, both in color and composition. However, in looking at other space films - like Alien and a couple of the Buck Rogers films - we had noticed that the difference between those ships and the Star Trek ships was that the Star Trek ships were always shot with high ambient light, whereas in films like Alien the faces of the characters seem to be lit from the instruments themselves. With that in mind, we worked very hard to use brighter components on the instruments so that Don Peterman, the cinematographer, could use them to light the ship. We also wired everything so that they could be put into dimmers and we could change the color quickly. As a result, Don had to add very little of his own lighting; and what he did add was done so carefully that it still looks as though the characters are being lit by the instruments." Just barely acclimated to the Klingon vessel - which McCoy rechristens the H.M.S. Bounty- the Enterprise crew unanimously elects to leave the rocky, amber terrain of Vulcan and return to earth. Live-action plates of the Bird of Prey being prepared for the journey were shot with just a minimal ramp set on a Paramount parking lot covered with tons of reddish, claylike dirt and augmented with painted backdrops. The ship itself and the surrounding landscape were added by the ILM matte department from a painting by Frank Ordaz. A second matte painting was required for a subsequent multi-element shot of the Bird of Prey lifting off from the planet. In addition to the panoramic background - rendered by Sean Joyce - the shot included a motion control Bird of Prey, bluescreen footage of Amanda and Lieutenant Saavik observing the departure, rearprojected flame elements tied to ceremonial pillars in the painting and a backlit sun. In short, it presented more than the usual share of challenges for all concerned. "We liked the fact that

the shot had a pan in it," matte photography supervisor Craig Barron asserted, "because it added so much to it. But it also created technical problems that made the shot more difficult. We worked in some bluescreen material that wasn't really bright enough, for instance. But it's a good direction to go in, I think, putting more movement into these shots instead of always having a static matte shot. Cutting from a shot where there is a lot of movement going on to a static matte shot is too jarring, so in the shots we re doing now we try to add movement whenever possible." Several approaches were considered with regard to adding the pan. "One way would have been to pan off the foreground characters during the live-action," Barron explained. "Had we done that, though, it would also have been necessary to pan off the painting, pan off the foreground rocks, pan off the sun, pan off the Bird of Prey and pan off a fire element. Rather than try to match all those elements up and make sure that the pan rates were correct for each individual one, it was decided to shoot all the elements static and add the pan with a motion control camera." Matte cameraman Wade Childress was responsible for incorporating the all-important pan movement. "We determined the size of the painting by figuring out how far we could pan," Childress explained, "and since we used the full pan capability of the Automatte camera, we ended up with a very long painting - about four by twelve feet on canvas. The fire element was rear-projected into the painting between a couple of monoliths that are standing out on the plain. And as the camera pans across the painting, a small sun is revealed in the sky. To get the proper flare, we used a bare bulb for the sun and a small plano convex lens to focus the light. We focused the filaments of the bulb right onto the camera lens to get a real nice flare as the ship approaches the sun. So the camera was on one plane, the painting was replaced with the plano convex lens and the light was behind that. Parallax problems developed as we continued to pan across with the sun in front of us, so we had to program the lens to compensate for that - it remained focused on the sun as it came into frame." Eventually, all of these elements were put together in optical. "I'm very proud of the shot," admitted optical supervisor Ralph Gordon. "We had to take live-action bluescreen and a bluescreen bly diet save and a back ground matte paintient and not only did it another during the pan, but we also had to keep horrendous matte lines from popping up as we went back towards the sun. The sun in a shot like that provides a great blank field for mistakes to show up in, so we had to work with that quite a bit. The reflection of the sun in the element that was provided ended up exposing the matte box of the camera so we got a squarish-looking reflection. Vaseline helped us to diffuse the image and diminish the hard-edged look that it had." Since the light from the sun is so powerful that it tends to bleed around anything shot in front of it, the optical department strove to achieve that same effect by using two separately CINEFEX 29 • 7 TE 94 PR

photographed stage passes on the Bird of Prey. "First we had a normal color pass that was shot on stage. After that the stage crew draped everything around the ship in black and used just a key light to give us a yellow-orange highlight pass that matched the color of the sun. So as the ship lifted off, we'd start with the normal color pass. Then, as it passed by, we'd bring up the highlight pass and start getting a rim-light effect. Finally, as we complete the turn and the ship goes off toward the sun, we began physically dropping out the percentage of the holdout so that there wasn't one hundred percent holdout working against the sun. We had to make two passes - sixty percent with the matte and forty percent without - which essentially caused the sun to bleed through the ship a little bit. As a result, you see the powerful light of the sun coming through everything; and that effect really puts the ship into the scene." In many ways, the Vulcan shots covered old and familiar territory for both the optical and the matte departments - the pan shot, in fact, was almost identical in composition to one done earlier for Enemy Mine. However, new techniques and new philosophies are being explored all the time. "We always try to do the shots better than we did before," matte painting supervisor Chris Evans asserted, "and we are currently rethinking how best to design matte shots. Very often a shot is a storytelling element in the film - you want to say that this is here and that is there - and in putting those different elements together you compose the shot in a very orderly way. However, if you are out on location or a photographer covering a real story in the real world, you often shoot things that have unexpected compositions or are asymmetrical or are odd in some way - and they look real. So we're trying to strive for shots that are more unexpected and less contrived." Kirk and his followers take off from Vulcan totally unaware of Starfleet's mounting concern as the sinister alien probe advances undeterred through Federation space en route to earth. Establishing Starfleet Command's impressive headquarters - an artful blending of futuristic elements with recognizable present-day landmarks - was a task that fell again largely to the matte department. "The Starfleet Command matte shot had to convey a lot of information to the audience," Evans explained. "One, that it is an international futuristic headquarters for the planets; two, that there is a lot of activity, with people coming and going; and, three, that it is supposed to be San Francisco of the future. So you're trying to tell three different stories simultaneously. I knew it would be tough, but I was excited about pulling off a shot like that that was very complex and in broad daylight." Almost everyone in the matte department contributed a design for the shot; and as conceptual illustrator for the film, Ralph McQuarrie's input was also sought. "McQuarrie's design was a view of the headquarters building - but from much further back, looking down at the Golden Gate Bridge. His architecture was brilliant, but it was so far away that you didn't really see people moving around. We thought the shot would be stronger if people were prominent - you see people in costume, walking around, like you were really there and about to step into the building." As always, careful planning was required to insure that all the various elements could ultimately be blended into a successful and convincing composite. "To shoot the people walking around," Evans continued, "we needed a vast area of smooth, clean concrete which we found at the Oakland Airport near the AirCal terminal. We got thirty extras on the runway; and to make sure that their heads didn't go above the horizon where we wanted the building to be, we set up our camera about fifteen feet off the ground on a big scaffolding. We then shot through a hard-edged matte on glass so the people could walk behind the little shuttlecraft that was painted to look like it was sitting right in the middle of the plaza. Even the shadow of the shuttlecraft was a matte. The shuttle was put into it later so that it looked like it was actually sitting on the concrete with its shadow cast and people walking behind it. We even directed one of the actors to interact with the shuttlecraft - filling the gas tank or something, We had to tape out areas so that people could walk here and there without crossing behind matte lines, and the perspective was worked out very carefully." "It was a difficult shot for us, technically," Craig Barron agreed, "because we had to have a piece of glass in front of the camera and a matte that was in absolute sharp focus. If that edge was soft, there would be haze and a blend line as the people walked behind the shuttlecraft and the building - and we couldn't have that. So we had to figure out how big the glass had to be, how far away from the lens it had to be so that the matte would be at a certain f-stop and a certain degree of sharpness. Then other factors came up. We had essentially a big slab of concrete with a lot of backlit people on it. Do we try to fill in the shadows with light? Eventually we decided that it would be too difficult to set up arcs or reflectors to balance everything out. We might be able to balance the people in the foreground, but we certainly couldn't do the people that were thirty, forty or in some cases three hundred feet back. We'd planned the shot very carefully so that the people in the foreground loomed large and the people in the distance looked very small in comparison so there'd be that relationship to give it depth. A painting, after all, is just a flat piece of artwork and the only way to get depth into it is with the live-action." Ultimately, the matte department was disappointed with the shot. "I had really high hopes for it," Evans confessed, "but something happened to it along the way and to me it doesn't quite have the sparkle of reality. We probably put more design effort into that one shot than any shot we've ever done, but it was just really hard to pull off because it was in broad daylight and seventy-five percent of the frame was a painting. Plus the very subject matter of the shot didn't help. With a painted building, there's no motion there to give it life." Craig Barron offered another suggestion as to why the shot was not as successful as they had hoped. "There may have been just too many things in it," Barron observed. With the headquarters now established, the action moves inside where Admiral Cartwright tries to make sense of the probe's bewildering and seemingly passive usurping of power from his Starfleet vessels. As Cartwright confers with his aides, behind him is a huge window revealing the San Francisco skyline and the Golden Gate Bridge. A marrying of live-action and bluescreen imagery, the panoramic view of the city was assembled in optical. "The matte department provided the painting of the skyline," Ralph Gordon explained, "and the stage provided a shuttlecraft that flies by. A field recorder had been used for the live-action plate; so when we went to shoot the background painting, we were able to put that same information into the computer system. That way, theoretically, there would be the same move in both. We found, however, that there was a glitch in the system and we had to take what the computer said was correct and throw it one frame out of sync on either side to see if we slowed down or accelerated the movement. As the move began, the focus changed - following actor Brock Peters and throwing the window out of focus. For the shot to look right, we had to find a way to throw the background painting out of focus as well. To do it, we had to optically rack focus about one hundred and twenty frames of film - which meant that our operator had to physically readjust the focus that our operator frame by frame. We figured at what point Brock Peters started moving towards camera and at what point the camera settled and stopped focusing and then we tried moving the lens about 10/1000s of an inch per frame, just as a place to start. We're hooked up to computers so we can deal in those fine increments. After a few attempts, we got it." Included in the environs of Starfleet Command's earth headquarters is the space dock - a model which, like the spaceships, had been used in a prior Star Trek film. "The space dock had been one of our bigger projects for Star Trek III," said Jeff Mann. "But at the end of that show Paramount had told us to trash it. We thought it was a very nice set - it had miles of fiber optics and all kinds of time-consuming things on it - so we took it apart as carefully as we could and stored it. Sure enough, it showed up again in Star Trek /V, so we had to put it all back together. We were very glad we saved it, though, because it was a major undertaking originally." The lights of the space dock go black as the probe neutralizes all of its power. As the probe draws nearer to earth the oceans begin to vaporize and tumultuous storm clouds fill the sky. "The swirling clouds were a combination of cloud tank effects and baking soda on black velvet," Don Dow explained. "Although, in actuality, the movement of a hurricane is not evident from outer space, we tried originally to get a hurricane formation by putting the baking soda on the velvet in a hurricane formation and then rotating it. But that was a little too static, so we added some cloud tank footage where we had swirled the water around and then injected paint into it. We thought we might have to project the cloud tank material onto a dome to create a curvature; but as it turned out, the altitude of the shot was high enough that we were able to get by with just a flat look. We did shoot the clouds on slightly different planes, though, and changed our camera angle to simulate the curve of the earth. Mattes were generated from the cloud tank material which was then matted into the painting of the earth." The storm mounts in violence as the probe wreaks havoc with the earth's atmosphere. Lightning bolts - often an animation effect - were shot on stage in keeping with the show's 'effects incamera' philosophy. "We set up little rheostatted light bulbs and shot them slow-motion. They were done on black velvet and then superimposed. We determined where the clouds would be in the shot and we had certain areas where we just used a little light on a stick, held it out and rheostatted it up and down. The lightning was then just double-exposed into the shot." A plume of water shoots up from the ocean as the probe continues its transmission into the sea. Dow's first inclination was to get the shot by actually going out into the ocean and laying down primer cord to produce a geyser-like stream of water. However, concern by the Fish and Game Commission regarding the safety of area sea life led him to create the effect through other means. "We set up a trough that was about twenty feet long and painted it glossy black. Then we filled it with tiny glass beads that are made by 3M to paint reflective lines on highways. The camera was turned upside-down and we opened the trough and let the beads fall out. The trough was on a bit of a slant so the beads slid down it - but, of course, upside-down it looked like they were shooting up in the air. Then we added a cloud tank element to make a cloud appear as the water was rising up and an animated sparkle on the water which is supposedly the energy coming from the probe. Actually, that sparkle helped to cover up our match. We couldn't get a very good match at the water's surface because nothing was really happening in our water plate. So that bit of animation helped to cover the area where we had to make the blend." Heretofore oblivious to the plight of their native planet, Admiral Kirk and his comrades pick up the distress signal sent by the Federation president. Within minutes, Spock has identified the probe's signal as being akin to the song of the humpback whale, extinct for centuries. (Evidently no one on earth thought to put a Vulcan on the problem.) In desperation, Kirk conceives a radical plan - a journey through time to the twentieth century to procure a pair of humpback whales that, hopefully, can satisfy the probe's dauntless quest. The resulting time

travel passage was one of the most extensive effects sequences in the film - encompassing motion control miniatures, animation, computer generated imagery and major optical work. As scripted, the crew's against-the-odds journey through time could be realized only if they were able to get the Bird of Prey to a speed of warp ten - a feat the ever-pessimistic Scotty considers highly improbable - and then slip past the sun in a daring acceleration-boosting maneuver designed to piggyback off its enormous gravitational pull. Though ILM animators were by now seasoned veterans of the warp drive effect - a signature of the Star Trek films - the trailing point-of-view of the Bird of Prey shot made it more difficult than the standard Enterprise warp drive to which they were accustomed. "Usually, the Enterprise streaks off and is gone so fast that you really don't see anything," said animation supervisor Bruce Walters. "But this shot was much trickier because the warp drive had to keep coming off the Bird of Prey. Not only was the ship going away from us at a slow speed, but we were right behind it and the POV was changing, As the ship was going away from us, we needed the texture in the warp drive to be coming toward us at a fast speed. Another factor that made it tricky was that the tail of the ship was changing a little bit in perspective as it rocked back and forth in the shot. Charlie Mullen created the warp drive, plotting out the ship for the head end of the warp drive and then guessing at where the tail end would be. It was just a matter of trial and error." A more distant shot of the ship as it makes its slingshot manuever around the sun required another warp drive effect, produced by Jay Riddle of the animation department. "Jay employed slitscan techniques using artwork pieces from various parts of the ship. Taking that artwork and different colored gels and ripple glass, he matched the moves of the ship in the frame and then created streaks off of the different sections." Originally, the animation department was also slated to create the flaming orange sun that fills the frame as the Bird of Prey passes around its backside. However, an already overbooked schedule demanded that the project be delegated elsewhere and the effect was ultimately achieved on stage via a method devised by assistant cameraman Pete Kozachic. Generating computer graphics entails four basic steps: digitizing an object to produce a computer representation of it in three dimensions; animating the object frame by frame to produce a suitable choreography for the shot; rendering the object by computing the sequence of images and incorporating the elements of color and texture and light; and finally, scanning the imagery out onto film. They have their subject sit in front of a video camera for about ten or twenty seconds, either rotating around on the chair or having a camera rotating around them. That way, their computer captures a full threedimensional description of the subject. Normally that data is then sent to an automatic milling machine that takes styrofoam and in a few hours mills out an actual bust. "So you get these little beams following the contours. The video camera is in between the two beams; and as the person turns, the camera sees these two contours tracing out around his head. Each frame of video sees a bright line with some shape. Ultimately, the system winds up producing a series of radial cross-sections of the person's head and the resulting data is 256 by 512 data points - which is all the resolution you'd want to have a face scanned out at. More than that and you pick up wrinkles and other imperfections. It was really ideal for our purposes." A slide contact mount was used - with the missiles being slid onto a rail-like mount and then electronically triggered via wires inside the aircraft. When ignited, the miniature missiles would fire down the rail and, once airborne, follow a fairly straight trajectory into a net set up to catch them. 'We had to experiment with a number of different types of flash charges to get the right density of smoke and flame to match the footage of the one real - but unarmed - missile that the Navy allowed their pilots to fire for the live-action crew." Ultimately, Stolz used hobby rocket engines that were enhanced to produce a larger burst of flame by putting a flash compound into the tail and then covering it over with a thin layer of plasticine clay. "It was very simple really. One of the things you begin to find out as you work more and more in this field is that the simple things tend to work best. You don't have to get exotic if you just think about what you are trying to accomplish and test for it methodically." As with any pyrotechnic work, safety consciousness was always at the forefront. "Generally you spend more time on safety factors than you do on the actual pyrotechnics," said Stolz. "You want to be certain that the explosive device goes off when you want it to and that it is isolated from any outside interference. On Top Gun, there really wasn't much danger except when we were experimenting with some things. But there are always unpredictable elements. Occasionally, pieces would chip off and go flying in the wrong direction, so we used fire retardant outfits and hoods whenever we got into dangerous areas. And we always had people standing ready with fire extinguishers and hoses. You can never forget about the risks involved. Through testing you try to minimize the variables, but you can never completely control the characteristics of explosions - so safety is always paramount. A pyrotechnician with fingers The Top Gun pyrotechnic work dictated that certain of the models be recreated in whole or in part with special materials. "For various shots," explained Dave Sosalla, "the models had to be cast in materials other than those we used in just the flying shots. For example, one of the shots involved a wing and tail section being blown off, which had to be done without the rest of the plane being destroyed. To do that, the wing and tail were cast in lightweight fragmentable materials that would completely explode and fragment on screen. A number of these were cast so that the shot could be tried several times. We made wing and tail sections that were scored in such a way that they could be quickly and easily applied to the aircraft body after the pyrotechnics had been inserted internally." To help insure that the main body of the plane survived the detonations and was thus reusable for subsequent retakes, the fuselage and other nonexploding elements were cast in heavy-duty epoxy. Both miniature and optical effects were employed in some of the shots. "Tony had a shot planned where he wanted to see a Sidewinder missile streak through the frame and slice a wing off one of the MiGs," Sosalla recalled. "He then wanted another shot where that same plane was seen tumbling out of the sky with one wing blown off and the whole thing smoking and in flames. The first part of the shot was accomplished with remote control pyrotechnics in the wing and we suspended the plane from our eighty-foot manlift on a cable. The plane was cast in that same heavy-duty fiberglass epoxy, except for the explodable wing portion that was made out of the more fragmentable material which allowed us to keep resplicing wings onto the body until we got a good shot. As luck would have it, we got the shot on the first take." The approved explosion shot was then combined with special effects animation. "The Sidewinder missiles were created with artwork," explained animation supervisor William Groshelle. 'We took our explosion plate, put it in a rotoscope camera, projected it down onto animation paper and traced the action of the explosion. We then used that tracing as the basis for creating our animation artwork. The animated missile drawings were composited optically with a fifty percent density matte on the tail flames. We also added smoke elements and highlights that matched up the angle of the sun and the plane, complete with vibration streaks that matched the way the plane was vibrating in any given frame. So the Sidewinder shots required a combination of anywhere from two to eight elements per frame." A similar approach was employed to obtain a convincing representation of tracer fire. "Wes Takahashi, one of our animators, worked with Bill Groshelle on the creation of the animation artwork for the missile shots and the tracer fire," Gutierrez recalled. "Stuart Cudlitz also contributed to the sequence, as well as animation cameraman Donald Smith and crew members Loring Doyle, Sam Comstock and Carter Tomassi. We don't do our own opticals; so when the in-house work was finished, Bill went down to Modern Film Effects in Los Angeles and supervised the optical compositing. He was on top of all the wedge testing and so forth. We were very pleased with the way all those missile shots turned out, although we had to do some fudging around with the

densities of our matte elements to get them to look right." Animation was also responsible for simulating the computerized 'heads-up' targeting displays projected onto the inside of F-14 canopies so that pilots can see their electronic instrumentation while still looking straight ahead. "Our 'heads-up' targeting displays required up to five elements per frame," said Groshelle. "First we rotoscoped all of the second unit aerial footage - all of the motions of the airplanes going through their maneuvers - and then we choreographed motion control camera moves on different pieces of artwork designed to simulate computer graphic displays. Quite a lot of testing was required to make it look as though the plane was trying to elude our little boxes and circles, but it was all done after-the-fact with static artwork. Once the displays were finished, we densitymatted them over the aerial footage." As with the pyrotechnic and model effects, the apparent realism of Top Gun's animation offered a small, yet important, boost to the film's overall believability. Each of these elements - skillfully combined with heart-thumping live-action material - helped director Tony Scott and his producers serve up for moviegoing audiences a singular taste of the edge-of-your-seat excitement usually known only to fighter pilots. Gary Gutierrez and USFX had captured that same sort of excitement for The Right Stuff, so they were aware of the challenges facing them and drew upon past experience to meet new demands. The enormous popularity of Top Gun - far and away the year's boxoffice champion - and the fact that its miniature and animation work went by virtually unnoticed, proves that seamless special effects can be achieved without a multimillion dollar effects budget and an arsenal of computers. "At our company we have most of the bells and whistles that everyone else seems to have these days," Gutierrez concluded, "and I'm as appreciative as anyone when it comes to technological advances. But I think there's a tendency sometimes to latch onto a particular technology and try to use it in all circumstances. For me, satisfying the requirements of the film is more important than advancing the state of the art. Oftentimes it just isn't necessary to push the limits of technology. It's like vacuuming your carpets. How many times have you had a piece of lint that just wouldn't come loose - and yet you stood there running your vacuum cleaner over it and over it rather than simply reaching down and picking it up? Technology tends to do that to us. We become dependent upon it to the point where we overlook the obvious. There's no question that technology is great and that we should use it whenever we need it. But perhaps we should think about it first and see if the technology we have at hand is really appropriate to the job." Top Gun photographs copyright ® 1986 by Paramount Pictures Corporation.
